title: Bulgeless Evolution And the Rise of Discs (BEARD) II. The role of mergers in shaping the Milky Way analogues in TNG50
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures. Published in A&A as part of the BEARD project, https://beardsurvey.com
summary: We study the formation and evolution of bulgeless galaxies within the Milky Way-Andromeda analogue sample of the TNG50 simulation. Through kinematic decomposition with Mordor, we identified bulgeless galaxies with a bulge-to-disc mass ratio of B/D<0.08, in line with the Bulgeless Evolution And the Rise of Discs (BEARD) survey and Milky Way constraints. We compared them to bulge-dominated galaxies (B/D>1). We find that 74% of bulgeless galaxies experience at least one major merger (stellar mass ratio 1:4) over their lifetime. Bulgeless galaxies form later ($z_{50}\sim 0.7$) than bulge-dominated counterparts ($z_{50}\sim1.2$). Bulgeless galaxies have lower-mass haloes and higher specific stellar angular momentum, compatible with Milky Way observations. However, specific star formation rates and hydrogen gas fractions are slightly higher than Milky Way observations. Our analysis of the redshift evolution of stellar components reveals that bulgeless galaxies have gradual disc growth with high thin disc-to-total mass ratios (D/T>0.5) since $z\sim 1$ and minimal bulge growth (B/T<0.1) since $z\sim1.5$. In contrast, bulge-dominated galaxies have earlier disc formation, which is disrupted, resulting in higher morphology evolution. Bulgeless galaxies are more likely to undergo gas-rich, coplanar, and corotating mergers, promoting disc survival, compared to bulge-dominated galaxies that encounter a broader spectrum of mergers. We also observed differences in galaxy structure between bulgeless and bulge-dominated galaxies without major mergers, suggesting the relevance of early gas accretion and alignment. Bulgeless galaxies have younger stellar populations and more extended star formation histories than bulge-dominated galaxies, which rapidly quench and have older stellar populations. These findings elucidate the distinct merger-driven and secular pathways that give rise to Milky Way galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using TNG50 simulations, the authors study bulgeless galaxies (B/D<0.08) compared to bulge-dominated galaxies (B/D>1) in Milky Way-Andromeda analogues. They find 74% of bulgeless galaxies underwent major mergers, but form later (z~0.7), have lower-mass haloes, higher angular momentum, and distinct merger properties (gas-rich, coplanar, corotating) that preserve discs. Bulgeless galaxies show gradual disc growth and extended star formation histories, while bulge-dominated galaxies form earlier, experience disruptive mergers, and quench rapidly.
AI.motivation: To understand how bulgeless galaxies like the Milky Way form and evolve, particularly whether major mergers necessarily destroy discs or if specific merger conditions and secular processes allow disc survival and growth.
AI.method: Analyzed Milky Way-Andromeda analogues from TNG50 simulation, identified bulgeless galaxies via kinematic decomposition (Mordor) with B/D<0.08, compared to bulge-dominated galaxies (B/D>1), examining merger histories, halo properties, star formation rates, gas fractions, and structural evolution across redshift.
AI.result: 74% of bulgeless galaxies experienced major mergers. Bulgeless galaxies form later (z~0.7), have lower halo masses, higher specific angular momentum, and slightly elevated sSFR and HI fractions vs. Milky Way. They maintain high thin-disc fractions since z~1 with minimal bulge growth. Their mergers are preferentially gas-rich, coplanar, and corotating; bulge-dominated galaxies experience broader merger types. Even without major mergers, structural differences exist, suggesting early gas accretion matters.
AI.conclusion: Bulgeless galaxies can survive major mergers if mergers are gas-rich, coplanar, and corotating, alongside gradual secular disc growth. Distinct merger-driven and secular pathways explain the diversity of Milky Way-like galaxies.

title: Bulgeless Evolution And the Rise of Discs (BEARD) I. Physical drivers of the mass-size relation for Milky Way-like galaxies
summary: In the standard $Λ$ cold dark matter ($Λ$CDM) cosmology, the existence of massive pure-disc galaxies remains challenging within the hierarchical framework and is key to understanding the evolutionary history of Milky Way-like systems. In this work, we investigate the physical origin of the scatter in the stellar mass-size relation of massive spiral galaxies, with a particular focus on bulgeless systems. We analyse 22 nearby bulgeless galaxies from the Bulgeless Evolution And the Rise of Discs (BEARD) survey using deep $g$- and $r$-band imaging obtained with the 2.5 m Isaac Newton Telescope Wide Field Camera. We derive surface-brightness, colour, and stellar-mass-density radial profiles to measure $R_1$, the radius where $Σ_* = 1\,\mathrm{M}_\odot\,\mathrm{pc}^{-2}$, adopted here as a physically motivated size proxy. Point spread function (PSF) effects are corrected through star subtraction and wavelet deconvolution. BEARD bulgeless galaxies follow the tight stellar mass-$R_1$ relation defined in previous studies, with a similar scatter of $\sim 0.1$ dex. Using galaxies from the IllustrisTNG50 simulation, we find that the scatter is linked to morphology, with bulgeless, BEARD-like analogues and bulge-dominated galaxies tracing the upper and lower envelopes of the relation, respectively. This trend correlates with the specific central stellar mass density, $Σ^{\mathrm{spec}}_{1,\mathrm{kpc}}$, suggesting that differences between observations and simulations reflect the broader central-density range spanned by BEARD bulgeless galaxies. A deeper analysis of the physical driver of this morphological segregation reveals that the scatter in the mass-size relation is also related to the spatial configuration of merger events, rather than their frequency, with bulgeless systems tending to inhabit halos with a slightly higher spin. (abridged)

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why some massive spiral galaxies lack bulges (pure-disc galaxies) within ΛCDM cosmology. Using observations from the BEARD survey and IllustrisTNG50 simulations, the authors find that bulgeless galaxies populate the upper envelope of the stellar mass-size relation, with scatter linked to morphology, central stellar mass density, merger geometry, and halo spin rather than merger frequency.
AI.motivation: The existence of massive pure-disc galaxies challenges hierarchical galaxy formation models. Understanding the scatter in the stellar mass-size relation of massive spirals, especially bulgeless systems, is key to constraining the evolutionary pathways of Milky Way-like galaxies.
AI.method: 22 nearby bulgeless galaxies from the BEARD survey were analyzed using deep g- and r-band imaging from the 2.5 m INT WFC. Surface brightness, color, and stellar mass density profiles were derived, with R₁ (where Σ* = 1 M⊙ pc⁻²) as a size proxy. PSF effects were corrected via star subtraction and wavelet deconvolution. Comparisons were made with IllustrisTNG50 simulations.
AI.result: BEARD bulgeless galaxies follow the tight stellar mass-R₁ relation with ~0.1 dex scatter. In TNG50, the scatter correlates with morphology: bulgeless analogues trace the upper envelope, bulge-dominated galaxies the lower envelope. This correlates with specific central stellar mass density (Σ^spec_1,kpc). The scatter is linked to merger geometry and halo spin, not merger frequency.
AI.conclusion: The morphological segregation in the mass-size relation is driven by the spatial configuration of mergers (not their rate) and higher halo spin, offering a physical explanation for the existence of massive pure-disc galaxies in ΛCDM.

title: The Lumina Project: CMB Optical Depth Fluctuations from Patchy Reionization
comment: 20 pages, 20 figures. Submitted to OJA. Please visit https://lumina-simulation.com/ for more details
summary: Patchy reionization couples the ionized-bubble morphology to the underlying density field, making the CMB Thomson optical depth sensitive to both the global ionization history and anisotropic fluctuations on the sky. Using the large-volume radiation-hydrodynamical Lumina simulation, we compute $τ_{\rm CMB}$ in two ways: (i) from global volume- and mass-weighted ionization histories, and (ii) from explicit line-of-sight integrations through on-the-fly light cones. We find that the sightline-averaged optical depth in the light cone, $\langle τ_{\rm LOS} \rangle = 0.0550$, exceeds the value inferred from a global volume-weighted history, $τ_{{\rm CMB},V} = 0.0515$, by $\approx 7\%$. This enhancement is largely captured by the global mass-weighted prediction, $τ_{{\rm CMB},m} = 0.0544$, indicating that precision comparisons to CMB optical-depth constraints should use mass-weighted electron fractions or explicit light-cone integration rather than volume-weighted ionized fractions alone. The excess optical depth accumulates primarily near $z_{\rm LOS} = 8.0^{+1.9}_{-1.3}$, where the combination of high physical density and strong ionization-field patchiness is greatest. The resulting $τ_{\rm LOS}$ field is non-Gaussian and exhibits $\gtrsim 5\%$ sightline-to-sightline scatter, with fluctuations tracing rare early-ionized overdensities and large-scale structure. Coarse-graining experiments show that smoothing the ionization field on $\gtrsim 3 {\rm cMpc}$ scales suppresses the density-ionization correlation and biases $τ_{\rm CMB}$ low relative to the resolved calculation. Finally, angular power spectra and real-space correlation functions decomposed into HII, HeII, and HeIII auto- and cross-contributions reveal scale-dependent departures from simple hydrogen-helium co-tracing and evolving characteristic scales with redshift.

AI.tldr: Using the Lumina simulation, the authors find that the CMB optical depth derived from line-of-sight integration (τ=0.0550) is ~7% higher than from volume-weighted ionization history (τ=0.0515), matching mass-weighted predictions (τ=0.0544) better, with excess accumulating near z~8 and non-Gaussian sightline scatter >5%.
AI.motivation: To quantify how patchy reionization and density-ionization coupling affect the CMB Thomson optical depth, and to determine whether volume-weighted ionization histories are sufficient or if more sophisticated treatments (mass-weighted or light-cone integration) are needed for precision comparisons to CMB constraints.
AI.method: Using the large-volume radiation-hydrodynamical Lumina simulation, the authors compute τ_CMB via (i) global volume- and mass-weighted ionization histories, and (ii) explicit line-of-sight integrations through on-the-fly light cones, with additional coarse-graining experiments and angular power spectrum decomposition into HII, HeII, HeIII contributions.
AI.result: Sightline-averaged τ=0.0550 exceeds volume-weighted τ=0.0515 by ~7%, largely captured by mass-weighted τ=0.0544; excess optical depth accumulates near z=8.0; τ_LOS field is non-Gaussian with >5% sightline scatter; smoothing on ≥3 cMpc scales biases τ low; scale-dependent departures from simple H/He co-tracing are found in angular power spectra.
AI.conclusion: Precision comparisons to CMB optical-depth constraints should use mass-weighted electron fractions or explicit light-cone integration rather than volume-weighted ionized fractions alone.

title: The pre-infall bias of subhalos
summary: Dark matter halos destined to fall into a more massive host differ from typical field halos of the same mass even before infall. In cosmological simulations, we find that the progenitor mass functions of these "future subhalos" are systematically shifted toward higher masses, with the shift growing as infall approaches. The bias takes a compact form within extended Press-Schechter theory: the collapse barrier is multiplied by a function $β(D/D_\mathrm{infall},a)$, where $D$ is the linear growth factor at scale factor $a$ and $D_\mathrm{infall}$ is the growth factor at infall. We find $β(x,a)=(1-x)^{1.20+0.14a}$ for the $M_{200\mathrm{c}}$ mass definition and $(1-x)^{1.20+0.05a}$ for $M_{200\mathrm{m}}$; the explicit scale-factor dependence captures the late-time influence of dark energy. One consequence is that halos shortly before infall are 10-15% more centrally concentrated than typical field halos of the same mass.

AI.tldr: Future subhalos (destined to fall into a more massive host) have progenitor mass functions shifted toward higher masses compared to typical field halos. This bias is captured in extended Press-Schechter theory by modifying the collapse barrier with a function β(x,a) = (1−x)^(p+qa), where p≈1.20 and q depends on mass definition (0.14 for M200c, 0.05 for M200m). This leads to 10–15% higher central concentrations just before infall.
AI.motivation: Dark matter halos that are about to fall into larger hosts (future subhalos) differ from isolated field halos of the same mass, but this pre-infall bias has not been systematically characterized in a theoretical framework.
AI.method: Cosmological simulations used to compare progenitor mass functions of future subhalos vs. field halos; extended Press-Schechter (EPS) theory applied to derive an analytic correction factor β that multiplies the collapse barrier, parameterized as (1−x)^(p+qa) with x = D/D_infall.
AI.result: Progenitor mass functions of future subhalos are systematically shifted higher; EPS barrier correction β(x,a) = (1−x)^(1.20+0.14a) for M200c and (1−x)^(1.20+0.05a) for M200m; halos just before infall are 10–15% more concentrated.
AI.conclusion: The pre-infall bias of future subhalos can be compactly described within EPS theory via a scale-factor-dependent barrier modification, with observable consequences such as enhanced central concentrations.

title: Summary of Discussion Sessions from "The Dusty Universe 2025: The Fifth Pandust Conference"
comment: 61 pages, Summary of Discussion Sessions from "The Dusty Universe 2025: The fifth pandust conference", https://pandust2025.sciencesconf.org
summary: "The Dusty Universe: The Fifth Pandust Conference" took place in Tucson (AZ, USA) from November 10 until 14, 2025. The goal of this meeting was to get the dust community together to review where we are, hear exciting new results, and make plans for the future. The meeting encompassed all aspects of dust investigations including observations, theory, modeling, and laboratory studies. The conference consisted of invited review talks, contributed talks and posters. Science topics included interstellar dust (Milky Way & nearby galaxies), circumstellar dust (including Solar System & exoplanets), dust in Galaxies (including high-z), lifecycle of dust, and future needs (laboratory, theory, & observations), with a particular focus on results from JWST and ALMA, and on nanodust (including PAHs). On November 12th, we organized breakout discussion sessions covering a wide range of interesting dust-related topics. The purpose of this document is to capture the main topics/questions that were discussed, the key conclusions of these discussions, the challenges and possible solutions that were brought up, and the open questions that still remain to be answered. We hope that this document records our findings and challenges for the future generation.

AI.tldr: Summary of the Fifth Pandust Conference (Tucson, 2025) covering interstellar, circumstellar, and extragalactic dust; highlights results from JWST/ALMA and nanodust/PAHs; documents breakout discussion outcomes, challenges, and open questions for the future.
AI.motivation: To bring the dust community together to review current knowledge, share new results, and plan future directions in dust research.
AI.method: The conference included invited reviews, contributed talks, posters, and breakout discussion sessions covering observations, theory, modeling, and laboratory studies of dust across all astrophysical contexts.
AI.result: Key results from JWST and ALMA were highlighted; discussions yielded documented conclusions, challenges, possible solutions, and open questions for future dust research.
AI.conclusion: The document captures the state of the field and open challenges, intended as a record for future generations of dust researchers.

title: JWST Observations of Starbursts: Molecular Hydrogen Excitation and Disequilibrium in M82
summary: Emission from the pure rotational transitions of H$_2$ traces warm molecular gas, providing insight into its temperature distribution and local heating conditions. We have extended previous power-law H$_2$ temperature models to account for differential extinction by dust as well as non-equilibrium ortho-to-para-H$_2$ ratios (OPR). The turbulent environment of the M82 starburst offers a unique opportunity to study H$_2$ out of equilibrium conditions, using ~15 pc spatially resolved measurements from MIRI/MRS on JWST. With extensive detections of H$_2$ S(1)-S(7), we use our model to assess spatial variations in local heating conditions of molecular gas across a ~500 pc region of the M82 central starburst. The average slope of the recovered H$_2$ power law temperature distribution is consistent with prior studies, and the slope strongly anti-correlates with relative [Fe II]/H$_2$ S(1)-S(2) strength, pointing to the importance of shock-heating. Our models indicate that the OPR is, on average, about half of its equilibrium value. This suppression is attributed to cloud mixing timescales which are short compared to timescales for spin conversion, with molecular gas remembering its ''cooler past''. By accounting for OPR disequilibrium, we can identify instances of recent and rapid heating to better understand the flow of energy through the interstellar medium and track its thermal history.

AI.tldr: This paper models H₂ rotational emission in the M82 starburst using JWST MIRI/MRS data, finding non-equilibrium ortho-to-para ratios (OPR ~ half equilibrium) and anti-correlation between power-law temperature slope and shock indicators, revealing rapid heating and short mixing timescales.
AI.motivation: To understand the temperature distribution and local heating conditions of warm molecular gas in the turbulent M82 starburst environment, and to constrain the ortho-to-para ratio (OPR) and its departure from equilibrium.
AI.method: Extended power-law H₂ temperature models to include differential dust extinction and non-equilibrium OPR, applied to ~15 pc resolved JWST MIRI/MRS observations of H₂ S(1)-S(7) rotational lines across a ~500 pc region in M82.
AI.result: Average power-law temperature slope consistent with prior studies; slope strongly anti-correlates with [Fe II]/H₂ S(1)-S(2) ratio, indicating shock-heating; OPR is ~half its equilibrium value, attributed to short cloud mixing timescales versus spin conversion timescales.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for OPR disequilibrium allows identification of recent/rapid heating events and tracks the thermal history and energy flow through the interstellar medium.

title: Taking Inventory of the Most Promising Lensed Radio Sources for Constraining Fundamental Properties of Dark Matter
summary: While dark matter (DM) makes up roughly 80% of the total matter in the Universe, its microscopic properties remain one of the biggest questions in Cosmology today. Fortunately, those properties dictate the distribution and form of macro-scale gravitational structures in the universe, allowing for indirect studies which can distinguish between competing particle models. One such avenue for this research is via strong gravitational lensing systems, where dark halos in the lens substructure and along the line of sight perturb image positions and flux. However, the current population of sources suitable for this analysis is limited, especially at radio wavelengths where astrometric perturbations are observable. I will first discuss which properties of lens systems make them especially useful for DM constraints and examine the minimum amount of information necessary for such an experiment. Then, I present the results of two successful searches for new radio lenses in existing radio and optical surveys, utilizing a new method to expand the potential follow-up population for dark matter studies in the future. I conclude with a discussion of the completeness of this population.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses using strong gravitational lensing systems to study dark matter properties, presents new methods for finding radio lenses, and evaluates the completeness of the current lens population for DM constraints.
AI.motivation: Dark matter makes up ~80% of total matter, but its microscopic properties remain unknown. Strong gravitational lensing offers an indirect way to distinguish between competing DM particle models by observing how dark halos perturb image positions and flux.
AI.method: The author identifies lens system properties useful for DM constraints and determines the minimum information needed for such experiments. Two successful searches for new radio lenses are conducted in existing radio and optical surveys using a novel method to expand the follow-up population.
AI.result: Two successful searches for new radio lenses were completed, expanding the potential follow-up population for dark matter studies. The completeness of this lens population is assessed.
AI.conclusion: Strong lensing systems are valuable for DM studies, particularly at radio wavelengths where astrometric perturbations are observable. New methods can expand the limited lens population, though completeness remains a consideration for future dark matter constraints.

title: Peculiar velocities at low Galactic latitude
summary: The Laniakea Supercluster is the closest large scale structure of galaxies. Is such a structure expected in the standard cold dark matter model of cosmology? This would be a relatively simple question to answer, were it not for the fact that the Zone of Avoidance (ZOA) runs right through it. Recent improvements to this paucity of data in the innermost ZOA can be made from systematic 21 cm surveys using the MeerKAT telescope (e.g. Kraan-Korteweg et al. 2024), and implementing these HI-redshifts as an extension to the CosmicFlows4 database for reconstruction (Hollinger et al. 2026). In this paper we test the assumption that for the purpose of reconstruction, additional HI detected galaxies without peculiar velocity determinations could be placed at their Hubble distances. We present infrared photometry of 163 of these in HI detected MeerKAT ZOA galaxies, in addition to 2MASS Extended Sources in the ZOA to determine their peculiar velocities. Averaging these peculiar velocities into redshift bins, we find that peculiar velocity corrections in the Laniakea Supercluster ZoA region are not prohibitively large, and that one can proceed with its reconstruction using the copious redshift data now available.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether HI-detected galaxies in the Zone of Avoidance (ZOA) within the Laniakea Supercluster can be placed at Hubble distances for reconstruction purposes, finding that peculiar velocity corrections are not prohibitively large, validating the use of extensive redshift data for reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the Laniakea Supercluster, which is bisected by the Zone of Avoidance, is expected in the standard cold dark matter model, but the ZOA creates a data paucity that complicates reconstruction. Recent 21 cm surveys with MeerKAT provide new HI-redshift data, and the paper tests the assumption that these galaxies can be placed at Hubble distances for reconstruction.
AI.method: Infrared photometry of 163 HI-detected MeerKAT ZOA galaxies and 2MASS Extended Sources in the ZOA is used to determine their peculiar velocities. These velocities are then averaged into redshift bins to assess the magnitude of peculiar velocity corrections.
AI.result: Peculiar velocity corrections in the Laniakea Supercluster ZOA region are not prohibitively large, meaning the assumption of placing HI-detected galaxies at their Hubble distances is valid for reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: One can proceed with the reconstruction of the Laniakea Supercluster using the copious redshift data now available from MeerKAT HI surveys, as the peculiar velocity corrections are manageable.

title: Faraday Complexity and Depolarization in LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS-DR2) Polarized Radio Sources
summary: We present a broadband spectro-polarimetric analysis of 1,565 polarized radio sources from the LOFAR Two-Metre Sky Survey Data Release 2 (LoTSS-DR2) RM Grid catalogue. This study uses frequency-dependent Stokes Q and U spectra across the 120-168 MHz LOFAR HBA band to investigate their polarization properties. The polarization behaviour of each source is modelled with multi-component Faraday depolarization models to investigate the magneto-ionic environments responsible for low-frequency depolarization. Significant Faraday complexity is observed throughout the sample, with 43.2% of sources requiring two or three Faraday components. External Faraday dispersion dominates the depolarization behaviour, with 54.1% of sources classified as external-screen dominated and approximately 60% showing statistically significant evidence for turbulent external Faraday-active media, while only 10.3% are consistent with pure internal differential Faraday rotation. The intrinsic polarization angle and RM separations between fitted components are generally small, suggesting that many RM components trace physically related emission regions embedded within common magneto-ionic environments. A weak but statistically significant anti-correlation is detected between the polarization spectral index, $β$, and weighted Faraday dispersion, $σ_{\rm RM,wtd}$, for two-component systems, whereas one- and three-component populations show no significant trend. The rest-frame Faraday dispersion, $σ_{\rm RM,rest}$, exhibits significant positive correlations with redshift for the external-screen dominated and mixed depolarization populations, even after controlling for radio luminosity, indicating increasingly turbulent or strongly magnetized environments surrounding radio AGN at earlier cosmic epochs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a broadband spectro-polarimetric analysis of 1,565 polarized radio sources from LoTSS-DR2, modeling their frequency-dependent polarization with multi-component Faraday depolarization models. Key findings include significant Faraday complexity (43.2% need 2-3 components), dominance of external Faraday dispersion (54.1%), and a positive correlation between rest-frame Faraday dispersion and redshift, suggesting increasingly turbulent magneto-ionic environments around radio AGN at earlier cosmic epochs.
AI.motivation: To investigate the magneto-ionic environments of radio sources at low frequencies (120-168 MHz) by analyzing their depolarization properties, which probe the magnetic fields and thermal plasma along the line of sight.
AI.method: The authors used frequency-dependent Stokes Q and U spectra from LoTSS-DR2 to model polarization behaviour with multi-component Faraday depolarization models, classifying sources by depolarization type (external-screen dominated, internal, mixed) and fitting parameters such as Faraday dispersion, polarization spectral index, and RM components.
AI.result: 43.2% of sources require 2-3 Faraday components; 54.1% are external-screen dominated; ~60% show evidence for turbulent external Faraday media; weak anti-correlation between β and σ_RM,wtd for two-component systems; significant positive correlation between σ_RM,rest and redshift for external-screen and mixed populations, independent of radio luminosity.
AI.conclusion: The magneto-ionic environments of radio AGN become increasingly turbulent or strongly magnetized at earlier cosmic epochs, as evidenced by the redshift-dependent increase in rest-frame Faraday dispersion.

title: Recombination Thickness as an Uncertainty in Inflationary Observables
summary: Standard CMB analysis assumes a direct deterministic mapping between the multipole probed by the CMB $\ell$ and the primordial wavenumber $k$. Since the recombination era has a finite duration, this mapping is probabilistic by construction. We elevate the power spectrum of the primordial perturbations to a probability distribution caused by the finite duration of the recombination era. We show that a finite recombination width introduces a Gaussian smoothing scale in $\ln k$ with $σ_{\ln k} \sim σ_η/ D_*$, leading to a probabilistic mapping from multipoles to inflationary e-folds. This effect is zero in standard power-law inflationary scenarios, but it may become relevant for scenarios with exotic oscillating features of the primordial power spectrum, which will be probed by the future CMB experiments. The observed effective power spectrum is the true primordial spectrum blurred by the uncertainty in scale reconstruction, which is mathematically identical to a Bayesian marginalization over a latent variable, and thus there is a propagation of the measurement error in the independent variable, which is another more formal way to view the smoothing effect. Our results indicate that the smoothing has quantifiable effects on the spectral index and its running, but more importantly the difference between the TT and EE inferred spectral indices, $n_s^{TT}-n_s^{EE}$, is non-trivial, in contrast to standard inflation without smoothing, and might become observable by future cosmic microwave background experiments. Any tension in $n_s^{TT}-n_s^{EE}$ could indicate oscillations in the primordial spectrum and the effects of the power spectrum smoothing. Finally, a minimal Fisher matrix analysis is performed to investigate the observability prospects of the smoothing effect.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the finite duration of the recombination era introduces a probabilistic mapping between CMB multipoles ℓ and primordial wavenumbers k, creating a Gaussian smoothing in ln k space. While negligible for standard power-law spectra, this smoothing can significantly affect primordial spectra with oscillatory features. The effect is mathematically equivalent to Bayesian marginalization over a latent variable, and can produce non-zero differences between TT and EE inferred spectral indices (n_s^{TT} - n_s^{EE}) that future CMB experiments might detect.
AI.motivation: Standard CMB analysis assumes a deterministic ℓ-k mapping, but the recombination era has finite duration, making this mapping intrinsically probabilistic. This work aims to characterize how this finite-width effect smooths the reconstructed primordial power spectrum and whether it can be detected.
AI.method: The authors model the finite recombination width as introducing a Gaussian smoothing scale in ln k with σ_{ln k} ~ σ_η / D_*. They show the observed effective power spectrum is the true primordial spectrum blurred by scale reconstruction uncertainty, mathematically identical to Bayesian marginalization over a latent variable. A Fisher matrix analysis is performed to study observability.
AI.result: The smoothing effect is zero for standard power-law spectra but becomes relevant for exotic oscillatory features. The effect produces quantifiable modifications to the spectral index and its running, and most importantly, generates a non-zero difference n_s^{TT} - n_s^{EE} which cannot happen in standard inflation without smoothing.
AI.conclusion: Future CMB experiments might observe the smoothing effect via tension in n_s^{TT} - n_s^{EE}, which would indicate oscillations in the primordial spectrum. The smoothing is a fundamental consequence of finite recombination duration that cannot be ignored for non-standard primordial spectra.

title: AMPM II. A Lunar-Mass Primordial Black Hole Microlensing Candidate in the Milky Way Halo
comment: 18 pages, 20 figures, submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: Primordial Black Holes (PBH) are hypothesised to form during inflation and have long been considered a candidate for compact dark matter. Gravitational microlensing is known as a productive method for exoplanet discovery and characterisation, but also provides an experimental avenue to constrain the PBH abundance in the mass regime from $\sim 10^{-11}\ M_{\odot}$ to $\sim 10^5\ M_{\odot}$. We performed a high-cadence, optical microlensing survey with DECam over five nights towards the Large Magellanic Cloud, sensitive to microlensing timescales from minutes to days. Here, we report the discovery of an hour-long microlensing event. An optical depth probabilistic analysis indicates that the lensing object, which we refer to as Phoebe, is 5 orders of magnitude more likely to be part of the Milky Way's dark matter halo than part of the stellar content of the Milky Way and Large Magellanic Cloud. No matter the location of Phoebe, it is among the fastest and lowest mass microlensing signals ever detected, with an Einstein timescale of approximately 60 minutes. Using Bayesian modelling, we interpret Phoebe as a PBH with mass $0.032^{+0.227}_{-0.027} M_{\oplus}$, or approximately 3 lunar masses. Phoebe suggests a population of compact, lunar-mass objects associated with the dark matter distribution of the Milky Way, and potentially opens a new window to the physics of inflation.

AI.tldr: A high-cadence DECam microlensing survey towards the LMC discovered Phoebe, an hour-long microlensing event interpreted as a ~3 lunar-mass primordial black hole, 10^5 times more likely to reside in the Milky Way's dark matter halo than in known stellar populations, suggesting a population of compact lunar-mass dark matter objects.
AI.motivation: Primordial Black Holes (PBH) are hypothesised to form during inflation and are considered a candidate for compact dark matter; gravitational microlensing provides an experimental avenue to constrain PBH abundance in the mass regime from ~10^{-11} M⊙ to ~10^5 M⊙.
AI.method: A high-cadence optical microlensing survey using DECam over five nights towards the Large Magellanic Cloud, sensitive to timescales from minutes to days, with Bayesian modelling for mass interpretation.
AI.result: Discovery of an hour-long microlensing event (Phoebe) with an Einstein timescale of ~60 minutes; optical depth analysis shows it is 5 orders of magnitude more likely to be in the Milky Way's dark matter halo than in stellar populations; Bayesian modelling interprets it as a PBH with mass 0.032^{+0.227}_{-0.027} M⊕ (~3 lunar masses).
AI.conclusion: The discovery of Phoebe, an hour-long microlensing event, suggests a population of compact, lunar-mass objects associated with the Milky Way's dark matter halo, potentially opening a new window to the physics of inflation.

title: Memory burden effect of regular primordial black holes
summary: Primordial black holes (PBHs) have attracted intensive research interest as a promising candidate of dark matter. However, because of the Hawking radiation, the PBHs lighter than $10^{15}~\rm{g}$ have already evaporated before today. To extend the PBH mass window to small-mass range, two possible ingredients are explored. The first is the consideration of regular PBHs with non-singular metrics, which can decrease the Hawking temperature, thereby lowering black hole evaporation. The second is the incorporation of the memory burden (MB) effect, which can further suppress the evaporation rate, after regular PBHs have lost a certain amount of their initial masses. In this work, we combine these two ingredients and study the MB effects of three types of regular PBHs (the Hayward, Bardeen and Simpson--Visser black holes). Assuming a phenomenological self-similar evaporation, we find that the MB effect significantly relaxes the evaporation constraints. For a benchmark of the MB strength parameter $k=1$, a new PBH mass window opens at around $10^6$--$10^8$ g, where regular PBHs can compose all dark matter without violating the Big Bang nucleosynthesis bounds.

AI.tldr: This paper explores regular (non-singular) primordial black holes (PBHs) with memory burden (MB) effect to extend the PBH mass window to lower masses (around 10⁶–10⁸ g), where they can constitute all dark matter without violating evaporation constraints from Hawking radiation or Big Bang nucleosynthesis.
AI.motivation: Standard PBHs lighter than 10¹⁵ g would have evaporated by now due to Hawking radiation, limiting their viability as dark matter candidates. The authors aim to extend the PBH mass window into the small-mass range by combining regular (non-singular) black hole metrics with the memory burden effect that suppresses evaporation.
AI.method: The authors combine two ingredients: (1) regular PBHs with non-singular metrics (Hayward, Bardeen, Simpson–Visser black holes) which lower Hawking temperature, and (2) the memory burden (MB) effect, which further suppresses evaporation after the PBHs have lost a certain fraction of their initial mass. They adopt a phenomenological self-similar evaporation model to analyze the combined effects.
AI.result: For a benchmark MB strength parameter k=1, a new PBH mass window opens around 10⁶–10⁸ g, where regular PBHs can compose all dark matter without violating Big Bang nucleosynthesis bounds. The MB effect significantly relaxes the evaporation constraints on PBHs.
AI.conclusion: Combining regular black hole metrics with the memory burden effect allows PBHs in the 10⁶–10⁸ g range to survive to the present day and constitute all of dark matter, circumventing the usual evaporation limits from Hawking radiation and BBN constraints.

title: Prospect of Measuring the Cosmic Dipole by Strongly Lensed Gravitational Waves Associated with Galaxy Surveys
summary: The cosmic dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is traditionally interpreted as being caused by the observer's motion relative to the background. However, tensions with dipole measurements from radio galaxy counts motivate the need for independent probes. This work investigates the feasibility of using strongly lensed gravitational wave (GW) events to measure the cosmic dipole. Strongly lensed GWs produce multiple time-delayed images, which can be used to infer the distances to both the lens and the source. These distances, associated with the observed redshifts of the lens and the source from galaxy catalogues, encode information about the background cosmology and cosmic dipole effects. By reconstructing a statistical sample of doubly lensed GW events based on the singular isothermal sphere lens model, the cosmic dipole can be estimated jointly with background cosmological parameters. Using realistic simulations for Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, we forecast that a dipole magnitude $g$ consistent with both the CMB and number count measurement could be detected with 10 years of observation. Furthermore, constraints on $g$ are greatly improved by combining constraints from doubly lensed events with those from triply or quadruply lensed events. In the most optimistic scenario, where we measure the number count dipole magnitude with 10 years of observation, we obtain $g = (2.45^{+1.53}_{-1.28}) \times 10^{-3}$ from the combined constraint, provided that systematic uncertainties are mitigated. Although challenging, strongly lensed GWs offer a novel approach to measuring the cosmic dipole, providing an independent consistency test with different systematics from electromagnetic probes.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using strongly lensed gravitational wave events to measure the cosmic dipole, offering an independent consistency test with different systematics from electromagnetic probes like the CMB. Using simulations for Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, they forecast detecting a dipole magnitude consistent with both CMB and number count measurements within 10 years, with improved constraints from multiple-image systems.
AI.motivation: Tensions between the CMB dipole interpretation (caused by observer's motion) and dipole measurements from radio galaxy counts motivate the need for independent probes of the cosmic dipole.
AI.method: Using strongly lensed GW events with time-delayed multiple images to infer distances to lens and source. These distances combined with observed redshifts encode cosmic dipole and cosmological information. The dipole is estimated jointly with cosmological parameters using a statistical sample of lensed events based on the singular isothermal sphere model, with simulations for Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer.
AI.result: A dipole magnitude consistent with both CMB and number count measurements could be detected with 10 years of observation. Constraints improve significantly when combining doubly lensed events with triply/quadruply lensed events. In the most optimistic scenario, g = (2.45^{+1.53}_{-1.28}) × 10^{-3} from combined constraints.
AI.conclusion: Strongly lensed GWs offer a novel approach to measuring the cosmic dipole, providing an independent consistency test with different systematics from electromagnetic probes, though challenging.

title: Reassessing the Statistical Necessity of Stellar Velocity Anisotropy in Strong-Lensing Cosmology with Lens-by-Lens Photometric Constraints
summary: The stellar orbital anisotropy parameter ($β_{\rm ani}$) is a persistent systematic uncertainty in galaxy-scale strong gravitational lensing (SGL) cosmology. Typically fixed to isotropy or a local prior, it frequently degenerates with the lens density profile. We demonstrate this apparent redundancy largely arises from incomplete photometric constraints. We cross-matched 130 SGL systems with the Pantheon+ SN~Ia compilation, constructing a strictly matched sample of 107 SGL-SN pairs using a 5\% comoving-distance tolerance. Assuming a flat universe ($Ω_k = 0$), the distance ratio is derived from apparent magnitude differences between paired SNe~Ia, eliminating $H_0$ and absolute magnitude dependence without fitting explicit dark-energy models. To break the kinematic degeneracy, we incorporate lens-by-lens luminosity density slopes ($δ_i$) from high-resolution imaging. Adopting the quasi-model-independent P2 redshift-evolutionary framework ($γ(z) = γ_0 + γ_z z$), we find very strong statistical evidence for a free $β_{\rm ani}$. Fixing $β_{\rm ani}$ to isotropy ($β=0$) or a local prior ($β=0.18$) is strongly disfavored ($Δ\bic = 14.2$ and $48.9$) and artificially inflates intrinsic scatter. A complementary P3 framework ($γ(z,\tildeΣ) = γ_0 + γ_z z + γ_s \log_{10}\tildeΣ$) confirms these penalties ($Δ\bic = 13.5$ and $49.1$). Across all P2 variants, we consistently detect a negative redshift evolution of the density slope ($γ_z \approx -0.42$ to $-0.46$; ${\sim}1.5{-}2.0σ$), indicating ETG density profiles become shallower at higher redshifts. We conclude that when individual photometric constraints are incorporated, $β_{\rm ani}$ is statistically required as a free parameter to prevent severe dynamical modeling biases.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that fixing the stellar orbital anisotropy parameter (β_ani) in galaxy-scale strong lensing cosmology artificially biases results. Using 107 SGL-SN pairs from a cross-match with Pantheon+, the authors find that β_ani must be treated as a free parameter—fixing it to isotropy or a local prior is strongly disfavored (ΔBIC = 14–49). They also detect negative redshift evolution of the density slope (γ_z ≈ −0.42 to −0.46), indicating shallower profiles at higher redshift.
AI.motivation: The orbital anisotropy parameter β_ani is a persistent systematic uncertainty in SGL cosmology; it is usually fixed to isotropy or a local prior, degenerating with the lens density profile. The authors suspect this redundancy is largely due to incomplete photometric constraints rather than physical necessity.
AI.method: Cross-matched 130 SGL systems with Pantheon+ SN Ia compilation, yielding 107 SGL-SN pairs (5% comoving-distance tolerance). Used distance ratios from apparent magnitude differences to eliminate H₀ and absolute magnitude dependence. Incorporated lens-by-lens luminosity density slopes (δ_i) from high-resolution imaging. Applied quasi-model-independent P2 (and P3) redshift-evolutionary frameworks with β_ani as a free parameter.
AI.result: Fixing β_ani to isotropy (β=0) or a local prior (β=0.18) is strongly disfavored (ΔBIC = 14.2–49.1) and artificially inflates intrinsic scatter. Negative redshift evolution of density slope (γ_z ≈ −0.42 to −0.46, ~1.5–2.0σ) is consistently detected across P2 variants.
AI.conclusion: When individual photometric constraints are incorporated, β_ani is statistically required as a free parameter to prevent severe dynamical modeling biases.

title: Arm morphology in off-centre barred galaxies
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. Abstract abridged. English not edited
summary:
Many barred galaxies, including the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), display strong lopsidedness and off-centre bars. The dynamical connection between bar-disc misalignments, internal mass asymmetries, and arm morphology is not yet fully characterised. We investigate how internal mass imbalances within the bar and global offsets between the bar and the centre of mass of the system modify the equilibrium-point structure and the invariant manifolds that organise arms.
  We construct a barred galaxy model which includes an off-centred and asymmetric in shape bar. Using numerical continuation, we track the position, stability, and bifurcations of the Lagrangian equilibrium points as functions of the displacement of the asymmetric mass component along the bar and of the offset between the bar and the system's centre of mass. For representative configurations we compute the invariant manifolds of planar Lyapunov orbits around unstable points and analyse the resulting arm structures. Internal bar lopsidedness and modest bar-disc offsets that keep the centre of mass inside the bar preserve the classical configuration with five equilibrium points, but strongly distort the associated invariant manifolds, producing two arms with different densities and shapes. The bar-disc offset reaches a threshold at the point at which the galactic centre of mass exits the bar ellipsoid, in which a pitchfork bifurcation removes the collinear unstable points and the system transitions to a three-equilibrium-point configuration in which a single unstable point and its associated manifold supports one arm.
  This framework is compatible with the observed correlation between off-centre bars and photometric lopsidedness, and it provides a dynamical explanation for the strongly asymmetric arm morphology of galaxies such as the LMC.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how off-centred, asymmetric bars in barred galaxies affect equilibrium points and invariant manifolds, finding that internal lopsidedness and bar-disc offsets produce asymmetric arm morphologies, with a threshold transition where the centre of mass exits the bar leading to a three-equilibrium-point configuration and single-armed structure, explaining features seen in galaxies like the LMC.
AI.motivation: The dynamical connection between bar-disc misalignments, internal mass asymmetries, and arm morphology in barred galaxies (e.g., the LMC) is not yet fully characterised.
AI.method: A barred galaxy model with an off-centred, asymmetric bar is constructed. Numerical continuation tracks Lagrangian equilibrium points as functions of mass asymmetry displacement and bar-disc offset. Invariant manifolds of planar Lyapunov orbits around unstable points are computed to analyse arm structures.
AI.result: Internal lopsidedness and modest offsets (with centre of mass inside the bar) preserve five equilibrium points but distort manifolds, producing two asymmetric arms. A threshold occurs when the centre of mass exits the bar ellipsoid, triggering a pitchfork bifurcation that removes collinear unstable points, transitioning to a three-equilibrium-point configuration with a single unstable point supporting one arm.
AI.conclusion: The framework explains the correlation between off-centre bars and photometric lopsidedness, providing a dynamical mechanism for asymmetric arm morphology in galaxies like the LMC.

title: Probing String-Theory-Inspired Topologies of the Early Universe through CMB Temperature and Polarization Anisotropies
summary: TeV string-mass-scale strings have been excluded experimentally at colliders, as their effects have not been observed at the Large Hadron Collider (CERN). On the other hand, higher-scale string theory, with mass scales typically close to the Planck scale, is often regarded as experimentally inaccessible due to the enormous energies required for direct tests, and far beyond the reach of present or foreseeable particle accelerators. Nevertheless, the early Universe may provide an indirect observational window for high-string scale through imprints left on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). In this work, building on previous studies, we reexamine temperature and polarization angular correlations as probes of the geometry and topology of the pre-inflationary Universe. We focus in particular on two-point correlation functions at large angular scales, where signatures of nontrivial spatial topology may survive as relics of primordial physics. We investigate the observational consequences of toroidal compactification and analyze their impact on the primordial power spectrum of the CMB provided by the Planck satellite. Within the current experimental and theoretical uncertainties, we identify a possible indication closely related to spatial-parity breaking, consistent with the presence of six spatial extra dimensions in the early Universe, compactified at the GUT epoch before the start of inflation. Finally, we extend our framework to B-mode polarization, highlighting its potential as a sensitive probe in forthcoming ground-based and space-borne experiments with unprecedented precision.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how high-scale string theory may leave imprints on the CMB through nontrivial spatial topology from toroidal compactification, finding possible evidence for six extra dimensions compactified at the GUT epoch via parity-breaking signatures in Planck data, and extending the analysis to B-mode polarization as a future probe.
AI.motivation: While low-scale string theory (TeV scale) is experimentally excluded by collider data, high-scale string theory (near Planck scale) is often considered untestable. The authors aim to show that the early Universe, specifically CMB anisotropies, can provide an indirect observational window for high-scale strings through geometric and topological signatures of pre-inflationary physics.
AI.method: The authors reexamine temperature and polarization angular correlations as probes of pre-inflationary geometry and topology, focusing on two-point correlation functions at large angular scales. They investigate the observational consequences of toroidal compactification and analyze their impact on the Planck satellite's primordial power spectrum. They also extend the framework to B-mode polarization.
AI.result: Within current experimental and theoretical uncertainties, the authors identify a possible indication of spatial-parity breaking in the Planck data, consistent with the presence of six spatial extra dimensions compactified at the GUT epoch before inflation.
AI.conclusion: High-scale string theory may be indirectly testable via CMB signatures. The six extra-dimensional topology is a viable explanation for observed parity anomalies, and B-mode polarization offers a sensitive probe for future experiments.

title: Interacting Dark Sector field theory with phantom crossing
summary: Recent results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) provide evidence for a dynamical dark-energy component, whose equation of state appears to have recently crossed the phantom divide. In this Letter, we present an interacting dark-energy model, grounded in field theory, that naturally accommodates such a double crossing. In our framework, fermionic dark matter is coupled via a Yukawa interaction to a tachyonic scalar field governed by Born-Infeld dynamics. The phantom crossing arises at the level of the effective dark-energy equation of state, while the underlying scalar-field dynamics remains nonphantom and well bounded. We confront our model with data including BAO from the DESI (DR2) survey, CMB distance priors from Planck 2018, and the latest Type Ia supernovae compilations, obtaining robust constraints across the different data combinations and reconstructing a recent double crossing of the phantom divide. Furthermore, under naturalness assumptions, the model expects an ultralight fermionic dark matter mass of order $1.9\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}$, suggesting a possible connection with new light particles in the dark sector and motivating future tests with cosmological perturbations.

AI.tldr: A field-theoretic interacting dark-energy model with tachyonic Born-Infeld scalar field and Yukawa-coupled fermionic dark matter naturally explains the recent phantom-divide crossing observed by DESI, yielding an ultralight dark matter mass of ~1.9×10⁻³ eV.
AI.motivation: DESI data suggests a dynamical dark-energy component has crossed the phantom divide; existing models struggle to accommodate this without instabilities, motivating a well-behaved field-theoretic framework.
AI.method: Construct an interacting dark-energy model with fermionic dark matter coupled via Yukawa interaction to a tachyonic scalar field with Born-Infeld dynamics; fit to DESI DR2 BAO, Planck 2018 CMB priors, and Type Ia supernova data.
AI.result: The model robustly fits all data combinations and reconstructs a recent double crossing of the phantom divide; predicts an ultralight fermionic dark matter mass of order 1.9×10⁻³ eV under naturalness assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a viable, stable field-theoretic explanation for the observed phantom crossing and suggests a possible connection with new light particles in the dark sector, motivating future cosmological perturbation tests.

title: Environmental Sculpting of Galaxy Structure at Fixed Stellar Mass: A Multi-Scale Analysis Across Cosmic Time using 3 Million HSC Galaxies
comment: 25 pages, 15 figures, resubmitted to ApJ after review, C. Igel and A. Ghosh contributed equally to this work
summary: The extent to which galaxy structure is shaped by environment beyond the local universe, once stellar mass is controlled, remains an open question in galaxy evolution. We address this challenge using an unprecedentedly large sample of $\sim$3 million galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program spanning $0.3 \leq z < 0.7$ with $\log(M/M_{\odot}) \geq 8.9$. We correlate a mass-independent bulge-to-total ratio statistic with large-scale overdensity maps and cluster catalogs, propagating structural parameter posteriors through a Monte Carlo framework to robustly assess significance. We confirm with $>5σ$ confidence that galaxy structure depends on environment at fixed stellar mass, but this dependence is secondary to stellar mass and varies with redshift, mass, and environmental scale. At $z < 0.5$, we detect no significant structural correlation with large-scale overdensity, but cluster galaxies show statistically significant bulge enhancement compared to mass-matched field galaxies, indicating cluster-specific processes such as ram-pressure stripping and cumulative tidal interactions dominate structural transformation at these epochs. At $z \geq 0.5$, massive galaxies exhibit bulge-enhancement across both cluster- and large-scale environments, while lower-mass systems show enhancement only in cluster environments. This indicates that environmental mechanisms operate across broader spatial scales at earlier cosmic epochs, and enhanced merger rates, group preprocessing, and cosmic web stripping augment cluster-specific processes. By separating into star-forming and quiescent subsamples, we find nearly flat trends within each, demonstrating that the observed environmental effects arise from coupled morphological and star formation transformations. These results collectively reveal the multi-scale, epoch-dependent nature of environmental effects on galaxy structure.

AI.tldr: Using ~3 million galaxies from HSC-SSP at 0.3≤z<0.7, this study confirms with >5σ that galaxy structure depends on environment beyond stellar mass, but this dependence is secondary to mass and varies with redshift, mass, and environmental scale. Cluster-specific processes dominate at z<0.5, while broader environmental mechanisms operate at z≥0.5, with coupled morphological and star formation transformations driving the observed trends.
AI.motivation: To address the open question of whether galaxy structure is shaped by environment beyond the local universe when stellar mass is controlled, using an unprecedentedly large sample.
AI.method: Correlated a mass-independent bulge-to-total ratio statistic with large-scale overdensity maps and cluster catalogs for ~3 million galaxies from HSC-SSP (0.3≤z<0.7, log(M/M⊙)≥8.9), propagating structural parameter posteriors through a Monte Carlo framework.
AI.result: Confirmed >5σ that environment affects galaxy structure at fixed stellar mass, but this dependence is secondary to mass. At z<0.5, only cluster galaxies show bulge enhancement. At z≥0.5, massive galaxies show enhancement in both cluster and large-scale environments, while lower-mass systems only in clusters. Separate analysis of star-forming/quiescent subsamples shows nearly flat trends.
AI.conclusion: Environmental effects on galaxy structure are multi-scale and epoch-dependent: cluster-specific processes (ram-pressure stripping, tidal interactions) dominate at z<0.5, while broader mechanisms (mergers, group preprocessing, cosmic web stripping) augment cluster processes at higher redshifts, with coupled morphological and star formation transformations underlying the observed trends.

title: AMPM I. A Targeted Search for Asteroid Mass Primordial Black Hole Microlenses
comment: 13 pages, 14 figures, submitted to MNRAS, comments welcome
summary: Gravitational microlensing is a powerful technique for constraining the abundance of dark matter in asteroid mass to supermassive primordial black holes at masses of $-11 \lesssim \log M/\mathrm{M}_\odot \lesssim 5$. In this work, we introduce a new high-cadence stellar microlensing survey in the Large Magellanic Cloud, AMPM. The primary goal of AMPM is to place constraints in the asteroid-to-planetary-mass regime of primordial black hole dark matter. We present the five nights of survey data, the microlensing detection pipeline, and the microlensing efficiency of AMPM. We explore the impact of the stellar distribution in the Large Magellanic Cloud on the microlensing detection efficiency and conduct a detailed analysis of second-order microlensing effects and the impact on the primordial black hole dark matter constraints. Our findings indicate that these second-order effects shift the maximum sensitivity of AMPM toward the lunar-mass black hole regime at $10^{-8} - 10^{-6} \, M_{\odot}$. From the five nights of data, we detect a single microlensing candidate and find that AMPM can constrain at the 95\% C.L up to 30\% of the Galactic primordial black hole dark matter distribution.

AI.tldr: AMPM is a new high-cadence microlensing survey in the Large Magellanic Cloud aimed at constraining primordial black hole dark matter in the asteroid-to-planetary-mass regime. Using five nights of data, it shifts sensitivity toward lunar-mass black holes and can constrain up to 30% of Galactic PBH dark matter at 95% C.L.
AI.motivation: To constrain the abundance of dark matter in the form of primordial black holes across a wide mass range (−11 ≲ log M/M⊙ ≲ 5), especially in the poorly-constrained asteroid-to-planetary-mass regime.
AI.method: Introduces AMPM, a high-cadence stellar microlensing survey in the Large Magellanic Cloud, including a detection pipeline and efficiency analysis. Explores the impact of stellar distribution and second-order microlensing effects on detection sensitivity.
AI.result: Second-order effects shift maximum sensitivity toward lunar-mass black holes (10⁻⁸–10⁻⁶ M⊙). One microlensing candidate is detected from five nights of data. AMPM can constrain up to 30% of Galactic PBH dark matter at 95% C.L.
AI.conclusion: AMPM demonstrates capability to probe primordial black hole dark matter in the lunar-mass regime, providing meaningful constraints on its abundance in the Galactic dark matter distribution.
